stubs.angle: In a classic three-layer application (presentation, business logic, data access), which layer should hold a rule such as 'orders over 1000 get a 5% discount'?
stubs.answerHinge: Business rules belong in the business logic (domain) layer, not in UI handlers or SQL, so that every entry point applies them and they can be tested without the UI or the database.

stubs.angle: In a clean architecture solution with Core, Infrastructure and Web projects, which project reference arrangement is correct for a repository used by the application core?
stubs.answerHinge: Dependencies point inward: Core defines the repository interface and references neither Infrastructure nor Web, while Infrastructure references Core and implements the interface.

stubs.angle: From a list of components (HTTP controller, message consumer, CLI command, SQL repository, SMTP email sender, payment gateway client), select all driven (secondary) adapters.
stubs.answerHinge: Driven adapters are called by the application through ports it owns (persistence, email, external services), whereas driving adapters such as controllers, consumers and CLI commands call into the application.

stubs.angle: A runnable snippet models Money as a plain class and compares two equal amounts, printing that the prices differ; find the line that breaks value-object semantics.
stubs.answerHinge: A value object is defined by its values and must have structural equality; a plain class compares by reference, so the fix is a record (C# 9 and later) or overridden Equals and GetHashCode.

stubs.angle: When does splitting commands and queries into separate models pay off, and when is it unnecessary complexity for a service?
stubs.answerHinge: CQRS pays off when read and write needs diverge (different shapes, complex domain logic on writes, very different load); for simple CRUD over one model it adds code and indirection with no benefit.

stubs.angle: A runnable Order aggregate enforces a maximum of three lines in AddLine but exposes its lines as a public List, and the caller ends up with four lines; find the defective line.
stubs.answerHinge: Exposing the mutable collection lets callers bypass the aggregate root and break its invariant; the collection must be a private field exposed as IReadOnlyCollection so all changes go through the root.

stubs.angle: Why is it recommended to modify only one aggregate per transaction and to reference other aggregates by identity, and how are rules that span aggregates handled?
stubs.answerHinge: An aggregate is the consistency boundary: its invariants are enforced atomically within it, while rules spanning aggregates are kept eventually consistent, which keeps transactions small and avoids contention and large object graphs.

stubs.angle: Select all statements about CQRS that are true: it requires event sourcing, it requires a separate read database, it separates the model used for updates from the model used for reads, a separate read store makes reads eventually consistent with writes.
stubs.answerHinge: CQRS only mandates separate read and write models; event sourcing and a separate read store are optional, and only when a separate store is used do reads become eventually consistent.

stubs.angle: Which statement correctly distinguishes domain events from integration events?
stubs.answerHinge: Domain events are handled in-process within the same bounded context, typically as part of the same transaction, while integration events notify other bounded contexts or services and must be published only after the transaction commits.

stubs.angle: Sales, Support and Billing all use the word 'Customer' with different attributes and rules; should the system have one shared Customer model, and what is the alternative?
stubs.answerHinge: Each bounded context should own its own Customer model expressed in its ubiquitous language, linked by identity and translated at the boundaries, because one canonical model couples all contexts and grows inconsistent.

stubs.angle: How would you keep the modules of a .NET modular monolith from silently coupling to each other as the team grows?
stubs.answerHinge: Boundaries must be enforced mechanically, not by convention: a public contract per module with internal implementation types, data owned per module (separate schema, no cross-module joins), and automated architecture tests in CI that fail on forbidden references.

stubs.angle: Your team proposes splitting the monolith into microservices because builds are slow and merge conflicts are frequent; how do you decide and what do you propose?
stubs.answerHinge: Slow builds and merge conflicts are solved by modularising the codebase and the build, not by distribution; extract a service only for a concrete need such as independent scaling, deployment cadence or team ownership, after module boundaries have proven stable.

stubs.angle: A company template forces every new service into four projects with a mediator handler per endpoint, and a small internal CRUD service is taking weeks; what do you decide and how do you handle the template owners?
stubs.answerHinge: Architecture should match domain complexity: a simple CRUD service warrants a lighter structure, while the decision is agreed and documented with the template owners, keeping a clear path to add layers if the domain grows.

stubs.angle: How does Conway's law affect where service and module boundaries end up, and how can an architect use it deliberately?
stubs.answerHinge: Systems mirror the communication structure of the organisation, so boundaries that cut across team ownership create constant cross-team coordination; aligning teams with bounded contexts (the inverse Conway manoeuvre) makes the intended architecture stable.

stubs.angle: Should every bounded context become exactly one microservice, and what goes wrong when a service spans several contexts or a context is split into many tiny services?
stubs.answerHinge: A bounded context is a natural upper bound for a service: a service spanning contexts mixes models and owners, while splitting a context into many services turns in-context transactions into chatty cross-service calls; split further only for concrete scaling or deployment reasons.

stubs.angle: Two microservices read and write the same tables in one database; what is the main architectural cost of this arrangement?
stubs.answerHinge: Sharing tables couples the services through the schema, so neither can change its data model or deploy independently; each microservice should own its data and expose it only through its API or events.

stubs.angle: Select the capabilities an organisation should have in place before adopting microservices, from a list mixing operational prerequisites with optional technologies such as event sourcing, Kubernetes or a different language per service.
stubs.answerHinge: Fowler's prerequisites are operational: rapid provisioning, basic monitoring and rapid automated deployment; specific platforms, event sourcing or polyglot languages are not prerequisites.

stubs.angle: A large .NET Framework monolith must be moved to a modern architecture without a feature freeze or a big-bang rewrite; outline your migration approach.
stubs.answerHinge: Migrate incrementally with the strangler fig pattern: put a routing facade in front, carve out one capability at a time behind an anti-corruption layer that shields the new model from the legacy one, and retire legacy parts only once traffic has moved.
